ideas.title: Brownian Bridge Box Score
ideas.paper: 2606.11760 — A Fast Gaussian Mechanism under Continual Observation, with Applications
ideas.pitch: The paper's actual result: for privately releasing a running cumulative sum that grows over time (the classic binary-tree/Gaussian mechanism for continual observation), querying any past partial sum normally costs O(log T) noise-term summation; the paper shows you can sample the correctly-correlated noise for ANY node in constant time by treating the tree's noise process as a Brownian bridge and interpolating directly. Build a single-file HTML demo framed as a live, privacy-noised running tally — e.g. a basketball team's cumulative point total or a poker player's cumulative net winnings ticking up event by event. Two panels race side by side: 'Naive tree mechanism' (visibly walks up/down O(log T) tree nodes summing noise, shown as an animated tree traversal) vs 'Brownian bridge' (instantly interpolates the noise value as a bridge between two known endpoints, shown as a continuous stochastic path snapping to sampled points). Slider for T (number of events) shows the naive method's per-query cost growing while the bridge method stays flat — literally making the paper's asymptotic claim visible and race-able. Pure client-side math (cumulative sums + Gaussian sampling + Brownian bridge interpolation formula), no backend needed.

ideas.title: Manifold Bender: See a Deepfake's Intrinsic Dimension Spike
ideas.paper: 2607.18770 — GLID: Gated Local Intrinsic Dimension Repairs the Blind Spots of Face-Forgery Detectors
ideas.pitch: GLID's actual finding: forged images bend the local manifold of a vision transformer's patch-token representations, and different generator families bend it at different depths — GAN artifacts peak at the last layer, diffusion artifacts peak mid-network — giving a training-free geometric detection signal (0.805 mean AUC on their 16-axis cross-generator benchmark, +0.084 AUC gain on generation axes). Build an interactive canvas demo where the user drags points on a 2D/3D synthetic point cloud (standing in for token embeddings) to locally 'fold' or 'crease' the manifold, while a live local-intrinsic-dimension estimator (simple correlation-dimension or nearest-neighbor MLE estimator, computable client-side) recolors nearby points in real time — showing LID spiking exactly at the crease, the same signal GLID uses to catch forgeries no detector was trained on. Include a toggle simulating 'GAN-style fold' (spike near one edge) vs 'diffusion-style fold' (spike in the middle) to mirror the paper's family-specific-depth finding. Fully self-contained HTML/canvas/JS, no ML model needed since it's a geometric-intuition toy, not a real detector.

ideas.title: Reward Shaping Arena
ideas.paper: 2608.08158 — A Unified Framework for Dynamic Reward Shaping in Reinforcement Learning
ideas.pitch: The paper's core (theoretical) claim is that dynamic reward shaping's optimality guarantees depend on the interaction between how fast the shaping signal adapts and how stable the underlying learner is — additive potential-based shaping can preserve optimal policies, but reward replacement or fast-adapting shaping can destabilize learning when combined with replay buffers/bootstrapped critics. Build a single-HTML-file grid-world game (tabular Q-learning runs fast enough to train live in-browser, ~10-30fps) where the player designs a 'reward shaping schedule' with sliders: shaping type (additive potential-based vs. reward replacement), adaptation speed, and whether experience replay is on. Watch the agent's live policy heatmap and cumulative-reward curve either converge cleanly to the optimal path (when using potential-based shaping, per the paper's theory) or thrash/diverge (fast adaptation + replay + non-potential shaping) — letting the player literally break and fix the theorem's preconditions and feel why they matter. Ties into the arxiv-scrape project's basketball/games angle by framing the grid world as a simple 'shot clock' navigation game.

ideas.title: SFT vs. RL: The Multi-Task Tug of War
ideas.paper: 2608.03573 — SFT Conflicts, RL Coexists: A Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Multi-Task Learning for LLMs
ideas.pitch: The paper's real, surprising result: fine-tuning an LLM on multiple tasks with plain supervised fine-tuning (SFT) causes severe task interference (updates are 'norm-limited' — big weight-magnitude conflicts that overwrite each other), while RL fine-tuning naturally produces sparse, near-orthogonal parameter updates per task ('variance-limited' by advantage normalization) that let tasks coexist without stepping on each other — motivating their proposed 'Parallel-RL' training paradigm. A video essay explainer: animate two toy 2D loss landscapes/gradient fields side by side, one showing SFT's task gradients as thick overlapping arrows canceling each other out, the other showing RL's gradients as thin, near-perpendicular arrows that barely interact — building the intuition for why 'more tasks = more conflict' is true for SFT but not RL, then landing on the practical takeaway (Parallel-RL) for anyone training multi-skill LLM agents. Strong hook for the ML-practitioner YouTube audience since 'why does my multi-task fine-tune get worse the more tasks I add' is a common real pain point.

ideas.title: Interpolation Roulette
ideas.paper: 2607.09547 High-Dimensional Interpolators Can Be Fragile: Heavy Tails and High-Dimensional Large Deviations
ideas.pitch: Single-file HTML/canvas/d3 toy that literally makes you feel the paper's result. The paper proves that ridgeless (min-norm interpolating) regression is statistically fragile in high dimensions -- accurate on average but with a heavy right tail of catastrophic prediction errors that decays only like n·log(n), versus ridge-regularized regression's much faster n^2 tail decay. Build a 'spin the wheel' simulator: generate synthetic high-dim linear data with heavy-tailed noise, fit ridge and ridgeless models thousands of times client-side, and animate each trial as a spin landing on a live-updating histogram/roulette wheel of held-out prediction errors. Ridge trials cluster tight and boring; ridgeless trials mostly look identical but every so often the wheel lands on a huge spike bar -- a visceral 'accurate on average, fragile in the tail' moment. A slider for dimension/sample-size ratio (d/n -> 1) lets you dial fragility up live, directly reproducing the paper's large-deviation regime.

ideas.title: Spectral or Not? A Fractal Fourier Playground
ideas.paper: 2607.23071 Spectrality of Moran-Type Measures Generated by Two-Element and Three-Element Digit Sets
ideas.pitch: The paper's result: for these Moran-type (generalized Cantor) measures, spectrality -- whether the measure admits an orthogonal basis of pure exponentials, i.e. is 'playable' like a Fourier signal -- is completely determined by counting 2-factors and 3-factors in the zero set of the Fourier transform of each convolution term, even without the classical Hadamard-triple crutch. Build an interactive canvas: user picks a 2- or 3-element digit set and contraction ratio, sees the resulting fractal measure rendered on one side and a live plot of the zero set of its Fourier transform on the other, with a running tally of 2-factors/3-factors that predicts (per the paper's characterization) whether the set is spectral. Stretch goal: sonify the exponential basis functions when spectral is true, so you can literally hear a 'spectral' fractal versus a mute non-spectral one -- turns an abstract harmonic-analysis theorem into something you drag, watch, and listen to. Doubles as a great short YouTube explainer script once built.

ideas.title: TubeAlpha: Fintuber Sentiment-Divergence Signal
ideas.paper: 2311.15247 Information Content of Financial Youtube Channel: Case Study of 3PROTV and Korean Stock Market
ideas.pitch: The paper finds real, non-trivial alpha in a Korean financial YouTube channel: positively-mentioned stocks spike pre-announcement then crash (pump-and-dump pattern), negatively-mentioned stocks underreact and drift down post-announcement, and -- most interesting -- shifts in the channel's sentiment *tone relative to its own historical baseline* forecast Korean market portfolio returns, a signal that survives controlling for news sentiment, short-term rates, and liquidity risk. Build a pipeline (yt-dlp transcripts + LLM sentiment scoring + backtest against KOSPI/individual tickers) that computes each fintube channel's baseline-deviation tone signal and per-stock mention flags, ships first as a research dashboard, then productizes as a paid signal feed for retail/quant traders following Korean (and eventually US) financial YouTubers -- a domain nobody is systematically quantifying yet.

ideas.title: Kronecker Condition Number Lab
ideas.paper: 2607.12286 Structured Preconditioning in Affine-Invariant Geometry: Projection, Certificates, and Kronecker Separation
ideas.pitch: The paper proves that the closest Kronecker-structured projection A⊗B of a matrix is NOT always the one that minimizes the Hessian-relative condition number, gives a computable 'marginal-mismatch residual' certificate that detects this gap and points toward improvement, and shows 2x3 is the smallest matrix size where this separation strictly occurs. Build a small-matrix playground: sliders build/perturb a PD matrix, live panels show its naive Kronecker projection, that projection's condition number, the residual certificate value, and (toggle 'show counterexample') the paper's minimal 2x3 case where projection-optimal and condition-optimal diverge, with an arrow showing the descent direction the residual implies. Turns an abstract optimization/certificate result into something you can drag around and visibly break -- niche audience but a satisfying 'aha' for anyone who's fought preconditioners.

ideas.title: Slippage Anatomy: Where Your Uniswap Fee Really Goes
ideas.paper: 2309.13648v2 — Don't Let MEV Slip: The Costs of Swapping on the Uniswap Protocol
ideas.pitch: A single-page swap simulator that decomposes the total cost of a trade into its three real components straight from the paper: gas, benign price-impact slippage, and adversarial (MEV/sandwich) slippage. Sliders for trade size and pool choice (USDC-ETH vs PEPE-ETH) drive a stacked bar that animates as you drag — small trades show gas dominating, large trades show price-impact taking over, and switching to the PEPE pool bumps the adversarial-slippage slice ~80% higher than USDC, matching the paper's headline empirical finding. Underlying math is just a constant-product AMM curve plus a synthetic adversarial-probability function calibrated to the paper's reported ratio, so it's pure client-side arithmetic — no chain calls needed. Great 'feel the invisible tax' artifact for crypto Twitter.

ideas.title: CWLATE Playground: Watch a Fuzzy Cutoff Lie to You (and Get Fixed)
ideas.paper: 2602.01417v1 — Identification and Estimation in Fuzzy Regression Discontinuity Designs with Covariates
ideas.pitch: An interactive scatterplot with a draggable discontinuity threshold (framed as a sports/games cutoff — e.g. 'does crossing a minutes-played or win-total threshold cause a bonus/promotion') where treatment 'compliance' is noisy near the cutoff, exactly the fuzzy-RDD setting the paper studies. Toggle between the standard fuzzy-RDD Wald estimator and the paper's proposed Compliance-Weighted LATE (CWLATE, which weights by squared first-stage discontinuity), and watch the two estimates and their confidence bands live-update as you inject more compliance heterogeneity across a discrete covariate group slider — visibly reproducing the paper's core claim that CWLATE has lower MSE and more stable estimates when compliance varies across groups. All local-linear regression and bootstrap CIs run in-browser on synthetic data; no backend needed. Directly useful groundwork for the user's own NBA-props/threshold-effect modeling interests.

ideas.title: Risk-Controlled Sentinel: A Calibrated Real-Time Safety Monitor for LLM Output Streams
ideas.paper: 2607.02510v1 — Online Safety Monitoring for LLMs
ideas.pitch: The paper's finding is deliberately unglamorous but useful: a dead-simple monitor — take a scalar signal from an external judge/verifier model, threshold it, and calibrate that threshold with conformal/risk-control guarantees — matches fancier sequential-hypothesis-testing monitors on math-reasoning and red-teaming benchmarks. Build a lightweight wrapper library (a few hundred lines) that sits between an app and any LLM API: it scores each response with a small judge model, maintains a calibration set, and computes a threshold that provably bounds the false-negative (missed-unsafe) rate at a chosen risk level, alarming/flagging in real time when scores drift past it. Ship it as a pip-installable middleware plus a small HTML dashboard showing the live score stream, the calibrated threshold line, and the running empirical risk — a direct, low-effort upgrade path for something like the user's own Sage/Sentinel bot infrastructure, which already has error-forwarding plumbing to hook this into.

ideas.title: The Golden Width: An Interactive Averageness-of-Faces Beauty Toy
ideas.paper: 2602.13368v3 — The Influence of Width Ratios on Structural Beauty in Male Faces
ideas.pitch: A procedurally-drawn schematic face (canvas/SVG, no real photos needed — avoids the paper's own noted 'manipulation artifact' problem) whose interocular-distance-to-face-width ratio is controlled by a single slider spanning the paper's low/medium/high bins. As you drag, a live 'predicted attractiveness' curve peaks at the medium/average ratio the paper's Bayesian model identifies as most beautiful, visually replicating the 'averageness correlates with higher perceived attractiveness' result. Add a quiz mode that runs the actual two-alternative-forced-choice task from the study (two faces, pick the more attractive one, ratios randomized) and tallies your personal bias against the population curve at the end. Doubles as a tight, self-contained YouTube short concept ('I recreated a face-beauty psychology study — do you actually like average faces?') since the whole build is one HTML file and immediately shareable/quiz-bait.

ideas.title: Incidence vs. Prevalence: Flatten-the-Curve Lab
ideas.paper: 2511.00138v1 — Incentives for self-isolation based on incidence rather than prevalence could help to flatten the curve
ideas.pitch: The paper's SIS + imitation-dynamics model shows equilibrium prevalence only depends on isolation cost and time-in-isolation, but switching the isolation *trigger signal* from prevalence (how many are sick now) to incidence (new cases/day) meaningfully flattens the epidemic curve during the transient/early-outbreak phase, even though it doesn't change the long-run equilibrium. Build a single-page toy: an SIS compartmental sim running live (canvas line chart of I(t) and new-cases(t)), with a slider population that 'decides' to self-isolate based on either a prevalence threshold or an incidence threshold, using simple imitation-dynamics update rules for isolation adoption. Two side-by-side curves race in real time — user drags the cost/behavior-sensitivity sliders and literally watches the incidence-triggered population produce a lower, wider peak than the prevalence-triggered one, then watches both curves converge to the *same* equilibrium prevalence, exactly matching the paper's counterintuitive claim ('this matters for the sprint, not the marathon').

ideas.title: Break & Grab: The DNA End-Tethering Race
ideas.paper: 2605.24987v1 — DNA end tethering through break-induced DNA-protein condensation
ideas.pitch: The paper's core result is that after a DNA double-strand break, proteins near the break flip into a 'condensate-competent' state, and whether the two broken ends actually get tethered together is a kinetic race between polymer relaxation (ends diffusing apart via Rouse/Brownian motion) and condensation (proteins gluing them via liquid-liquid phase separation) — a race the cell reliably wins despite randomness. Build a canvas toy: two polymer chains (bead-spring, simple Brownian dynamics) with a 'break point' in the middle; a condensation-probability field switches on at t=0 and grows around the break; sliders control the relaxation rate vs. the condensation-onset/growth rate. Run many trials at once (ghost trails) to show a live success-rate meter — user drags the two rate sliders and watches the phase diagram emerge in real time: fast condensation + slow relaxation = ends reliably captured, and the reverse = ends drift apart and never re-meet, visually reproducing the paper's central kinetic-competition claim.

ideas.title: Shortcut Charging: Race the Capacitor
ideas.paper: 2605.18473v2 — Accelerating charging dynamics of electric double-layer capacitors
ideas.pitch: Using the Poisson-Nernst-Planck model, the authors derive time-dependent 'shortcut to adiabaticity' voltage protocols (polynomial voltage ramps) that cancel out an arbitrary number of relaxation modes, letting an EDLC reach full charge in a driving time comparable to or shorter than its natural RC time — roughly an order of magnitude faster than a standard step-voltage charge. Build a single-file toy that solves a simplified 1D PNP system (finite differences on ion density + potential between two plates) in the browser, animates the ion cloud building up at each electrode, and lets the user race two protocols side by side: a plain step voltage vs. the derived polynomial shortcut. A live surface-charge-density readout shows the shortcut protocol slamming into equilibrium ~10x faster, directly visualizing the paper's headline number in a way anyone can feel by watching the ion clouds snap into place.

ideas.title: Latent Breeder: Disentangled ML for Precision Agbio
ideas.paper: 2410.19922v1 (Compositional Autoencoder for genotype/environment disentanglement, 5-10x better trait prediction) + 2602.23269v2 (HATTER active-learning human-in-the-loop enzyme function prediction, competitive accuracy at a fraction of the labeling cost)
ideas.pitch: Seed companies and biotech labs both suffer from the same disease: models tangled up by confounded data (genotype x environment interactions in crop trials; sequence-to-function gaps in enzyme engineering) and expensive labels (multi-site field trials; wet-lab functional assays). Package both papers' actual mechanisms into one SaaS: a compositional-autoencoder module that splits any genotype x environment phenotype dataset into clean genotype-specific and environment-specific latent factors (replicating the paper's 5-10x lift on traits like Days-to-Pollen and Yield on maize panels), fused with an active-learning querying loop (à la HATTER) that tells a breeder or protein engineer exactly which next field trial or enzyme assay to run to most reduce model uncertainty. Pitch to seed companies (Corteva/Bayer-scale precision breeding budgets) and enzyme-engineering biotechs; tonight's demo is a synthetic-data landing page with a slider-driven latent-space visualizer (PCA-style scatter that visibly separates into genotype vs. environment clusters as you 'disentangle') plus a mocked active-learning query queue.

ideas.title: The Counterwork Engine
ideas.paper: 2606.27486 - Jarzynski equality for counterwork under reversed memory-filtered driving
ideas.pitch: A single-page Langevin-dynamics toy (canvas + JS Euler-Maruyama integrator) simulating a colloidal particle dragged through a moving harmonic trap, the classic optical-tweezer setup used to test Jarzynski's equality. Drag a slider to set the protocol speed λ(t); the page fires hundreds of stochastic trajectories and builds a live histogram of work values W, whose exponential average ⟨e^-W⟩ converges to the true ΔF (shown as a dashed ground-truth line) — the textbook Jarzynski result. Then hit 'Reverse' to apply the paper's sign-inverting memory kernel, generating the effective protocol Λ(t) that reverses the endpoints of λ(t); a second histogram of counterwork C appears, and a live readout shows ⟨e^-C⟩ landing on the reciprocal of the forward average (ΔF_C = -ΔF_W) plus a running check of the paper's Jensen-derived inequality ⟨C⟩+⟨W⟩≥0 — the user can try to crank sliders to break the inequality and watch it refuse to go negative on both sides. Lets a stat-mech audience literally feel a fairly abstract free-energy inequality instead of reading it.

ideas.title: Groundcheck: Fidelity Audits for LLM Credit Explanations
ideas.paper: 2608.08126 - Accurate Ensembles, Fragile Narratives: Multi-Scale Stacking and a Fidelity Audit of LLM-Generated Explanations for Credit Risk
ideas.pitch: The paper builds a strong credit-risk ensemble (ROC-AUC 0.9539) but finds its LLM-generated adverse-action narratives are dangerously unreliable: cases where the model 'named three factors as risk-increasing that the supplied attributions scored as risk-reducing, omitted the dominant driver, and introduced a feature never given to it,' with SHAP/LIME disagreeing substantially and calibration failing acceptable thresholds. Their conclusion — verification must happen post-generation, prompt engineering can't fix it — maps directly onto a live regulatory pain point (ECOA/Reg B require specific, accurate reasons for credit denial, and regulators are actively scrutinizing AI-generated adverse-action letters). Groundcheck is drop-in middleware that sits between a lender's model/attribution pipeline and its LLM narrative generator, running the paper's own audit methodology (sign-flip detection, omission detection, hallucinated-feature detection, cross-method attribution agreement, calibration/stability scoring) on every generated letter before it ships, blocking or flagging mismatches and producing a compliance-ready audit trail. Monetized per-audited-explanation or as a compliance subscription for banks/fintechs.

ideas.title: Broken Gate: Spot the Agent
ideas.paper: 2607.18659 - Broken Gates: Re-evaluating Web Bot Defenses in the Age of LLM Agents
ideas.pitch: An interactive canvas game replaying a handful of animated mouse-movement/click-timing traces and asking the visitor to classify each as human or LLM-agent-driven — dramatizing the paper's headline finding that 'challenge-based defenses are broadly ineffective against commercial solvers, which achieve near-perfect bypass at negligible cost' and that 'two agents with nearly indistinguishable behavioral footprints yield divergent outcomes.' After each guess, the demo reveals the twist: behaviorally the traces really are near-identical, but a hidden 'behind the curtain' panel shows the actual signals (headless flag, WebDriver property, TLS/JA3 fingerprint, execution-environment noise) that determined whether a real CAPTCHA system would have passed or blocked it — illustrating the paper's core claim that current bot gates key off environment authenticity, not behavior. Highly shareable 'can you spot the bot' format built on procedurally generated jittery-human vs. bezier-smooth-bot cursor paths, no backend needed.

ideas.title: Query Budget: Approximate-Sampling Visualizer
ideas.paper: 2606.11437 - The Power of Test-Time Training for Approximate Sampling
ideas.pitch: A small interactive tool that makes the paper's two theoretical results tangible on a toy discrete state space (bit-strings or graph nodes). It runs a classic random-walk sampler against a noisy density oracle (noise level ε controlled by a slider) and plots oracle-query count needed to hit a target error — tracing out the paper's proven quadratic (1/ε²) lower bound and showing the random-walk method sitting right on that optimal curve. Flipping a 'bounded class F' toggle switches to a test-time-training-style search over a small finite candidate list of distributions instead of blind random walking, and the second curve visibly breaks through the quadratic wall with far fewer queries — the paper's key finding that TTT surmounts the general lower bound precisely when the distribution class has bounded size. A live side-by-side chart makes an otherwise dry query-complexity proof into something you can watch happen.

ideas.title: Feel the Disorder Threshold — Scattered Data Interpolation Breakdown
ideas.paper: 2607.22968v2 — Isoperimetric-Combinatorial Bounds for Range-Controlled Matchings and Quasi-Interpolation from Scattered Data
ideas.pitch: Single-file canvas demo: a lattice of reference points Y at spacing h sits under a set of scattered/jittered points Q, jitter radius r controlled by a slider. The demo computes a live matching between Q and Y (animated connecting lines) and reconstructs a quasi-interpolated surface from Q's samples of a known test function, plotting reconstruction error against ground truth in real time. Below the paper's threshold r ≤ Ch, the interpolation stays smooth and converges at the claimed O(h^s) rate as h shrinks; push r past the threshold (a Hall-type cube-population imbalance) and the matching visibly snaps/tangles and the reconstruction error blows up — letting you literally feel the isoperimetric-combinatorial cutoff the paper proves, not just read about it.

ideas.title: Grow the Grains — Live Persistent Homology for Point Patterns
ideas.paper: 2607.09228v1 — Central Limit Theorems for Functionals of Persistence Diagrams in Germ-Grain Random Set Models
ideas.pitch: Single-file canvas toy: scatter 'germ' points under a chosen spatial process (Poisson/CSR, clustered, or hard-core repulsive — toggle switch), then animate a slider growing a disk of radius t around every point (the germ-grain model). Track Betti numbers live via union-find (b0) and Euler characteristic on a rasterized grid (b1 proxy), plotting a real-time Betti curve/APF-style functional. A built-in Monte Carlo null (many CSR simulations) produces a z-score/'p-value' band so the user can watch clustered or repulsive patterns statistically diverge from random exactly as the paper's breast-tissue goodness-of-fit test does — a hands-on feel for topological GoF testing on spatial data.

ideas.title: Embedding Audit — trust scoring for biological foundation models
ideas.paper: 2602.22289v2 — What Topological and Geometric Structure Do Biological Foundation Models Learn?
ideas.pitch: The paper's 141-hypothesis battery found real signal in scGPT/Geneformer embeddings (persistent homology significant in nearly every layer, manifold-aware distance beats Euclidean for regulatory gene pairs) but showed it's uneven: strong in immune tissue, collapsing in lung, and two independently-trained models agree on the embedding's global shape (canonical correlation 0.80) yet disagree on precise gene placement (72% retrieval accuracy). Turn that battery into a productized audit: biotech/pharma teams fine-tuning or querying a bio foundation model for target discovery submit their tissue/cell-type context and get back a 'trust report' — which gene-neighborhood claims are statistically robust under null controls vs which are noise for that specific tissue — before committing wet-lab budget to a 'discovered' relationship. A picks-and-shovels QA layer for the fast-growing bio-FM market.

ideas.title: The Square-Root Wall: Why Some Certificates Can Never Get Better
ideas.paper: 2607.12134v1 — The Certification Limits of KS-Type Layer Relaxations: A Square-Root Ceiling and Its Breakdown
ideas.pitch: Pop-math explainer on convex-relaxation certificates: KS-type layer relaxations (assigning costs to individual layers plus pairwise couplings to bound a system's deficit) can never certify more than roughly √N no matter how cleverly they're built — a clean, animatable impossibility result. The twist that makes the video: for geometric systems like Lennard-Jones particle interactions, that ceiling doesn't just hold, it collapses to a linear-deficit regime and then to total uselessness past a threshold. Visualize with an animated chain of coupled springs/dominoes for the generic case, then morph into a jittering 2D particle lattice for the Lennard-Jones breakdown — 'the proof that knows its own limits' framing in the vein of a Quanta/3Blue1Brown deep dive.
